content: 1. A study by Nilsson (2014) found that the association between prenatal exercise and miscarriage risk was no longer statistically significant when adjusted for confounding factors. 2. Zhang (2011) reported a protective dose-response effect of exercise on miscarriage risk in a case-control study (cases: n=267; controls: n=285), after adjusting for potential confounders. 3. In contrast, Maconochie (2007) found no association between different levels of exercise and miscarriage risk in a case-control study (cases: n=603; controls: n=6116), even after adjusting for factors such as maternal age, year of conception, previous miscarriage, and previous live birth. 4. Ussher (2015) indicated no effect of prenatal exercise on the odds of stillbirth after adjusting for recruitment center as a stratification factor. 5. Magnus (2008) found no effect of exercising more than once per week on the odds of stillbirth compared to no exercise in a study involving 59,573 participants. 6. Dumith (2012) reported no association between exercise and stillbirth after adjusting for maternal age, marital status, education level, family income, parity, prenatal consultations, and twin delivery. 7. Xu (2014) observed a protective effect of exercising for at least 30 minutes two or more times per week on miscarriage risk compared to no exercise, after adjusting for factors such as history of miscarriage, induced abortion, night shift frequency, staying up late, regular physical activity, smoking, and alcohol consumption. 8. A systematic review by Davenport et al. (2019) concluded that prenatal exercise is not associated with fetal mortality, based on a meta-analysis of available data. 9. Kariminia et al. (2004) reported similar rates of cesarean section between a walking group and a pelvic rocking exercise group in a study comparing different exercise interventions during pregnancy. 10. Banerjee et al. (2013) demonstrated a protective effect of abdominal exercises on diastasis rectus abdominis measured three days postpartum compared to routine antenatal exercise. 11. A systematic review by Du et al. (2018) found no significant difference in cesarean delivery rates between physical activity intervention groups and control groups among overweight or obese pregnant women. 12. Beetham et al. (2019) reported no association between vigorous-intensity exercise in the third trimester and adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. 13. A systematic review by Bennett et al. (2018) found that interventions designed to reduce excessive gestational weight gain can reduce the incidence of gestational diabetes mellitus. 14. Nakamura et al. (2019) found that physical activity during pregnancy is associated with a reduced risk of postpartum depression, based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. 15. Syngelaki et al. (2019) reported that diet and exercise interventions during pregnancy did not significantly reduce the risk of preeclampsia in overweight and obese women. 16. Yu et al. (2018) concluded that exercise during pregnancy can help prevent gestational diabetes mellitus, based on a systematic review and meta-analysis.
